messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rohan presents as a meticulously dressed 36-year-old accountant, though his starched collar cannot conceal the profound tension in his jaw and shoulders. He sought therapy after receiving a formal warning about his performance at work, a final blow after a painful divorce last year. He speaks in quiet, clipped sentences, struggling to explain the suffocating unease that has become the entire landscape of his life. The roots of this distress, he haltingly explains, are not in his recent hardships but in the silent, echoing violence of his childhood home. He cannot narrate the events sequentially, confessing that he lacks the words for what happened. Instead, the trauma lives in his body as a collection of sensory fragments: the sickening thud of a fist against the wall, the smell of stale whiskey, and the high, thin sound of his mother’s weeping behind a locked door.

These fragments are not memories he can choose to visit; they ambush him without warning. At his open-plan office, the sharp clap of a colleague dropping a heavy ledger on a desk can instantly trigger a full-body response. In that split second, the fluorescent office lights seem to dim, the air grows thick, and he is no longer a man at his computer but a small boy hiding at the top of the stairs. The terror is not a recollection but a fresh and immediate experience; his heart hammers against his ribs, sweat slicks his palms, and a wave of nausea rises in his throat. This sudden hijacking of his senses reinforces his deeply held conviction that he is fundamentally helpless, that he has no power to stop bad things from happening to him. The memory, in its raw, terrifying power, confirms the boy's fear as the man's reality.

This constant state of physical readiness has become his baseline. Rohan describes his body as being perpetually coiled, a spring wound tight and ready to react to the slightest danger. This hypervigilance is exhausting, making it impossible to concentrate on the complex spreadsheets that define his job. Every unexpected footstep in the corridor, every raised voice from a nearby cubicle, is perceived as an imminent threat. Living this way, day after day, has cemented a profound sense of misery. He looks back on his younger self as a different person, someone who could laugh easily, and has come to believe that his capacity for happiness was permanently destroyed in that house. The relentless physical tension serves as constant, irrefutable proof that he is broken beyond repair. This feeling of being physically besieged also makes the past feel closer, as if the tension in his muscles is a magnetic force pulling those terrifying, wordless images to the surface.

His worldview is dominated by a sense of pervasive injustice and personal powerlessness. He is certain that he is incapable of protecting himself and that the world is an inherently unsafe place where perpetrators, like his father, face no consequences for the damage they inflict. This belief system is not an abstract philosophy but the engine of his daily suffering. Because he believes he is helpless, he feels he has no choice but to remain constantly on guard, scanning every room and monitoring every sound. This appraisal directly fuels the exhausting hypervigilance that ruins his focus and poisons any chance of relaxation. Furthermore, this narrative of a dangerous world and his own victimhood keeps him mentally trapped in the past, ruminating on the injustice of it all, which in turn makes the intrusive memories more frequent and more potent.

The cycle has become entirely self-sustaining and has cost him almost everything. His ex-wife, he now understands, couldn't live with a man who flinched at her touch if she moved too quickly or who would go rigid with fear at the sound of neighbors arguing through the wall. She saw his hypervigilance as irritability and his avoidance of conflict as emotional absence. At work, he wears noise-canceling headphones for most of the day, an attempt to build a fortress against the auditory triggers of the office, but it has only isolated him from his colleagues. He came to therapy not with hope, but with the quiet desperation of a man who feels his last footholds crumbling away. His greatest fear, he admitted in their last session, is that his appraisal of himself is correct: that he is truly helpless, and that he is simply watching the final, inevitable collapse of his own life.
